stem: A 35-year-old woman with functional neurological disorder presenting as a functional gait disorder has been diagnosed after positive clinical signs. She has been symptomatic for 8 weeks and uses a walking frame. She accepts the diagnosis and asks about treatment. She has comorbid GAD managed with sertraline 100 mg daily.

data_table.History: FND gait disorder, 8 weeks. Accepts diagnosis. No prior physiotherapy.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Specialist physiotherapy using motor retraining with graded task-specific exercises
Increase sertraline to maximum dose and add CBT targeting underlying anxiety as the primary driver
Commence trauma-focused therapy as childhood trauma must be resolved first
Prescribe diazepam short course to demonstrate improvement is possible at this stage
Recommend inpatient neurorehabilitation for 2-4 weeks given functional impairment

stem: A 25-year-old woman with known left temporal lobe epilepsy (on levetiracetam 1500 mg BD, well controlled for 2 years) presents with a new seizure type. Her usual seizures involve an epigastric aura, lip-smacking, and 2-3 minutes post-ictal confusion. The new events involve prolonged bilateral thrashing lasting 10-20 minutes without post-ictal confusion, eyes closed, and pelvic thrusting. Video-EEG captures a 15-minute event showing no ictal correlate. Levetiracetam level is therapeutic. She recently separated from her husband.

data_table.Investigations: Video-EEG: no ictal discharge during 15-minute convulsive event. Interictal: left temporal sharp waves. Levetiracetam 42 mg/L (RR 12-46)
data_table.History: Known left TLE. New event type past 4 weeks.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of the new seizure type?

options.text: Diagnose PNES, explain the diagnosis, refer for seizure-specific CBT, and maintain current levetiracetam
Increase levetiracetam as breakthrough seizures may present atypically from a new focus
Add sodium valproate for broader seizure coverage as video-EEG may miss deep temporal events
Reduce levetiracetam as the events may represent medication-induced behavioural disturbance
Arrange intracranial EEG monitoring to characterise the new seizure type definitively

stem: A 24-year-old woman with BPD and a history of multiple self-harm presentations arrives in the ED after superficial forearm lacerations. She is calm, oriented, not intoxicated, has a current DBT safety plan, reports using lacerations after intense distress, denies suicidal intent, and wishes to go home. Wounds require closure strips only.

data_table.History: Known BPD. Currently in DBT. No suicidal intent. Safety plan exists.
data_table.Examination: Superficial lacerations left forearm, not requiring sutures. Alert and calm.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ED management?

options.text: Admit involuntarily for suicidal self-harm requiring inpatient safety at this stage
Discharge after wound care with instructions to attend her next DBT session
Commence quetiapine 25 mg for emotional dysregulation to prevent future presentations
Provide wound care, collaboratively review her safety plan, contact her DBT team, and discharge
Arrange voluntary brief admission for 24-48 hours to allow emotional regulation

stem: A 30-year-old woman with BPD has been in standard DBT for 6 months. Her main remaining difficulty is responding to perceived rejection with intense rage followed by impulsive regretted actions. She recently sent a hostile resignation email to her supervisor after receiving constructive feedback. She identifies the pattern but cannot interrupt it.

data_table.History: BPD, 6 months in DBT. Completed mindfulness and distress tolerance modules. Currently in interpersonal effectiveness.

lead_in: Which DBT skill module most directly targets her described difficulty?

options.text: TIPP skills from distress tolerance for physiological de-escalation before action
Core mindfulness with emphasis on observing emotions without judgement
Interpersonal effectiveness DEAR MAN skill for assertive communication
Emotion regulation module focusing on Check the Facts and Opposite Action
Walking the Middle Path module focusing on dialectical thinking

stem: A 38-year-old woman with BPD is on quetiapine 200 mg nocte, sertraline 150 mg daily, and diazepam 5 mg TDS. She has been stable in DBT for 12 months, depression in remission 8 months, no self-harm for 10 months. She asks about medication review.

data_table.Medications: Quetiapine 200 mg nocte, sertraline 150 mg daily, diazepam 5 mg TDS
data_table.History: BPD, MDD in remission 8 months, no self-harm 10 months, stable in DBT 12 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate medication management approach?

options.text: Continue all unchanged as the patient is stable and change risks destabilisation at this stage
Switch quetiapine to lamotrigine for evidence-based BPD emotional regulation at this stage
Cease all three simultaneously as none are evidence-based for BPD and ongoing monitoring of progress
Gradually taper diazepam first, then review quetiapine, while maintaining sertraline for MDD relapse prevention
Increase quetiapine to 300 mg and add PRN benzodiazepine to replace scheduled diazepam

stem: A 27-year-old woman with BPD lives in regional NSW. She has recurrent self-harm and crises. No DBT program exists locally - the nearest is 3 hours away. She sees a GP fortnightly and has a Better Access psychologist offering general CBT. She will not travel for DBT. Her GP asks about locally deliverable evidence-based options.

data_table.History: BPD with recurrent self-harm. Regional NSW. No local DBT. Better Access psychologist available.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate locally deliverable treatment?

options.text: Standard CBT for BPD delivered by the Better Access psychologist with ongoing clinical monitoring
Structured clinical management through her GP with psychoeducation, crisis planning, and consistent boundaries
Telehealth DBT delivered by a metropolitan therapist under Better Access at this stage
Monthly psychiatrist telehealth with medication optimisation as primary treatment at this stage
ACT delivered by the local psychologist as a DBT alternative with appropriate specialist oversight

stem: A 21-year-old man is brought to the ED by police after being found running into traffic stating people were trying to kill him. He has been smoking high-potency cannabis daily for 3 years. Urine drug screen is positive for THC only. He is paranoid, disorganised, and responding to auditory hallucinations. This is his first psychotic presentation. He has no psychiatric history. His brother was diagnosed with schizophrenia at age 19.

data_table.Investigations: UDS positive THC only. BSL 6.2. Normal FBC, UEC, TFT, CRP.
data_table.History: Daily cannabis 3 years. First psychosis. Brother has schizophrenia. No prior psychiatric contact.

lead_in: What is the most important factor in distinguishing cannabis-induced psychosis from a primary psychotic disorder with cannabis comorbidity?

options.text: Resolution of psychotic symptoms within one month of cannabis cessation without ongoing antipsychotic requirement
Positive urine drug screen confirming recent cannabis use as the causative agent at this stage
Absence of negative symptoms such as flat affect and social withdrawal at presentation
Family history of schizophrenia confirming genetic predisposition to primary psychosis
Predominantly visual rather than auditory hallucinations suggesting substance-induced aetiology

stem: A 19-year-old man is brought to the ED by ambulance after smoking a substance purchased as 'herbal incense'. He is agitated, tachycardic, hypertensive, and vomiting. He has had two generalised tonic-clonic seizures en route. His friends report he smoked the product 90 minutes ago. Standard urine drug screen is negative for THC.

data_table.Investigations: UDS negative for all standard panels. BSL 7.8. VBG pH 7.31, lactate 4.2. CK 1840 U/L.

lead_in: What explains the negative THC result despite suspected cannabinoid exposure?

options.text: The patient likely consumed a different substance and is mistaken about what was smoked
The 90-minute interval is too short for THC metabolites to appear in urine at this stage
Herbal incense products typically contain non-cannabinoid substances such as cathinones
Synthetic cannabinoids are not detected by standard immunoassay THC screens which target delta-9-THC metabolites
The standard screen has insufficient sensitivity and would be positive if repeated in 6 hours

stem: A 26-year-old man presents to the ED for the fifth time in 3 months with cyclical severe nausea and vomiting. Each episode lasts 24-48 hours and resolves spontaneously. He reports that prolonged hot showers provide temporary relief. He has used cannabis daily for 8 years. Previous workup including upper GI endoscopy, CT abdomen, and coeliac serology has been normal. Standard anti-emetics have been ineffective.

data_table.Investigations: Previous: OGD normal, CT abdomen normal, coeliac screen negative. This visit: Na 134 mmol/L, K 3.2 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L (baseline 82)
data_table.History: 5 ED presentations in 3 months. Daily cannabis 8 years. Hot shower relief.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management strategy?

options.text: Advise complete cannabis cessation as the only intervention proven to prevent recurrence
Commence haloperidol 5 mg as a specific anti-emetic for cannabinoid hyperemesis episodes
Trial a proton pump inhibitor as the vomiting may represent atypical GORD despite normal endoscopy
Refer for capsaicin cream application to the abdomen as an evidence-based CHS-specific therapy
Prescribe ondansetron 8 mg TDS as prophylaxis between episodes at this stage

stem: A 17-year-old boy is referred by his school counsellor for cannabis use. He smokes 3-4 times weekly for 18 months. His academic performance has declined from top-quartile to failing two subjects. He sleeps until midday on weekends. He does not believe cannabis is a problem and says all his friends use it. He is not interested in stopping but has agreed to see you once.

data_table.History: Cannabis 3-4x weekly, 18 months. Academic decline. Low motivation. Pre-contemplative regarding change.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate therapeutic approach for this single session?

options.text: Commence structured CBT for cannabis use with goal-setting and trigger identification
Provide psychoeducation about cannabis neurotoxicity in adolescent brain development
Motivational interviewing exploring discrepancy between his values and current functioning
Recommend immediate abstinence and warn about academic consequences if use continues
Refer to a residential adolescent drug treatment program given the severity of academic decline

stem: A 22-year-old woman is brought to the ED from a music festival. She took two MDMA tablets 3 hours ago. She is agitated, diaphoretic, and confused. She is on sertraline 100 mg daily for anxiety but did not disclose this to her friends who provided the tablets.

data_table.Examination: Mydriasis, bilateral ankle clonus (>10 beats), hyperreflexia upper and lower limbs, diaphoresis, agitation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Administer dantrolene 1 mg/kg IV for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Administer cyproheptadine 12 mg orally stat as the specific serotonin syndrome antidote
Aggressive cooling, IV benzodiazepines for agitation, and IV normal saline for hyponatraemia
Restrict fluids for the hyponatraemia and apply external cooling only if temperature exceeds 40 degrees
Administer 3% hypertonic saline for symptomatic hyponatraemia and intubate for airway protection

stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the ED 8 hours after his last dose of GHB (gamma-hydroxybutyrate) which he has been using every 2-3 hours around the clock for 6 months. He is tremulous, diaphoretic, tachycardic, and increasingly agitated. He reports auditory hallucinations. He received diazepam 20 mg orally 2 hours ago with minimal effect. His GCS is 14. He is not responding to standard benzodiazepine doses used for alcohol withdrawal.

data_table.History: GHB q2-3h for 6 months. Last dose 8 hours ago. Minimal response to diazepam 20 mg.
data_table.Examination: Tremor, diaphoresis, agitation, responding to auditory hallucinations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer phenobarbital 15 mg/kg IV as GHB withdrawal does not respond to benzodiazepines
Escalate to high-dose IV diazepam titration in a monitored setting with ICU standby for potential intubation
Commence baclofen 10 mg TDS as a specific GHB receptor agonist for withdrawal management
Treat as alcohol withdrawal with CIWA-guided diazepam titration and thiamine supplementation
Administer sodium oxybate (pharmaceutical GHB) as substitution therapy with planned taper

stem: A 45-year-old man with stable schizophrenia on clozapine 400 mg daily wants to quit smoking. He smokes 25 cigarettes per day. His previous quit attempt with NRT patches failed after 2 weeks. His clozapine level is 420 mcg/L (therapeutic range 350-600). He has no history of seizures. His psychiatrist is planning to prescribe varenicline.

data_table.Investigations: Clozapine level 420 mcg/L. FBC: neutrophils 4.2 x10^9/L.

lead_in: What critical pharmacokinetic interaction must be monitored during the quit attempt?

options.text: Varenicline directly inhibits clozapine metabolism requiring clozapine dose reduction before commencing
Smoking cessation will increase clozapine levels via reduced CYP1A2 induction requiring dose reduction
Varenicline lowers seizure threshold synergistically with clozapine requiring prophylactic anticonvulsant
Nicotine replacement therapy must be ceased before starting varenicline due to nicotinic receptor antagonism
Clozapine must be switched to an alternative antipsychotic before a quit attempt due to toxic interaction risk

stem: A 52-year-old woman wants to quit smoking (20 cigarettes/day for 30 years). She has tried varenicline previously but developed nausea requiring cessation. She has no contraindications to NRT. She asks about the most effective NRT approach. She has a history of well-controlled hypertension on amlodipine.

data_table.History: 20 cig/day, 30 years. Varenicline intolerant (nausea). Hypertension on amlodipine.

lead_in: What is the most effective NRT strategy for this patient?

options.text: 4 mg nicotine gum alone as oral forms are more effective than patches for heavy smokers
21 mg nicotine patch alone as combination NRT increases cardiovascular risk in hypertensive patients
21 mg nicotine patch daily combined with 2 mg nicotine gum as needed for breakthrough cravings
Start with 14 mg patch and uptitrate to 21 mg if ineffective to minimise nicotine exposure
Nicotine mouth spray alone as it provides the fastest onset matching cigarette pharmacokinetics

stem: A 28-year-old woman who smokes 15 cigarettes daily presents at 12 weeks gestation. She has attempted behavioural counselling alone for 4 weeks without success. She asks about pharmacotherapy. She has no other substance use and no psychiatric history.

data_table.History: 15 cig/day. 12 weeks pregnant. Failed behavioural counselling 4 weeks.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy option?

options.text: 21 mg nicotine patch continuously as it provides the most consistent nicotine replacement
Varenicline as it has the highest cessation efficacy and no confirmed teratogenicity
Bupropion as it avoids nicotine exposure entirely while supporting cessation
Continue behavioural counselling only as no pharmacotherapy is safe in pregnancy
NRT intermittent-use forms such as gum or lozenge after discussing risks and benefits with the patient

stem: A 48-year-old man wants to quit smoking (30/day). He has tried NRT patches and gum (combination) with relapse at 3 weeks, and varenicline which he ceased after 1 week due to vivid nightmares and insomnia. He asks about bupropion. His medical history includes well-controlled type 2 diabetes on metformin and a single generalised seizure 8 years ago after heavy alcohol use (no recurrence, not on anticonvulsants, drinks 2 standard drinks per week now).

data_table.History: 30 cig/day. Failed combination NRT (relapse 3wk). Varenicline intolerant (nightmares). T2DM on metformin. Single alcohol-related seizure 8 years ago.

lead_in: Is bupropion appropriate for this patient?

options.text: Yes - the alcohol-related context means it was not a true epileptic seizure so the contraindication does not apply
Yes - a single provoked seizure from alcohol 8 years ago without recurrence does not constitute a seizure disorder
Yes - provided an EEG is normal and no anticonvulsant is required, bupropion can be used at reduced dose
No - bupropion is contraindicated due to his history of seizure regardless of the interval or context
No - but the reason is the diabetes, not the seizure history, as bupropion increases hypoglycaemia risk with metformin

stem: A 34-year-old woman is referred for ASD assessment. She reports lifelong difficulty with social relationships despite appearing socially competent. She describes exhaustion after social interactions, having learned to mimic facial expressions and small talk through conscious observation. She has intense interests in true crime and textile arts. She was a high-achieving student. She has been diagnosed with GAD, social anxiety, and depression over the years. Her daughter was recently diagnosed with ASD at age 6.

data_table.History: Previous diagnoses: GAD, social anxiety, MDD. Childhood: high-achieving but no friends. Conscious social mimicry. Daughter diagnosed ASD age 6.

lead_in: What clinical feature most strongly supports ASD rather than social anxiety disorder as the primary diagnosis?

options.text: Intense special interests in true crime and textiles distinguishing ASD from anxiety disorders
Comorbid generalised anxiety and depression supporting the neurodevelopmental theory of ASD
High academic achievement which rules out social anxiety as SAD impairs academic performance
Family history of ASD in her daughter confirming genetic predisposition at this stage
Conscious effortful mimicry of neurotypical social behaviour resulting in post-social exhaustion

stem: A 28-year-old man with ASD Level 1 (previously Asperger syndrome) presents to the ED with his support worker. He was in a shopping centre when the fire alarm sounded and he is now crouched in the corner, rocking, hands over ears, and non-verbal. He was physically uninjured by the alarm. He is not responding to verbal instructions. His support worker reports this has happened before and typically resolves within 30-60 minutes in a quiet environment. His vital signs are normal.

data_table.History: ASD Level 1. Known sensory overload episodes. Triggered by fire alarm. Non-verbal, rocking, hands over ears.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ED management?

options.text: Arrange psychiatric consultation for acute psychotic episode given his non-verbal state and abnormal behaviour
Administer midazolam 5 mg IM for acute behavioural disturbance as he is non-responsive at this stage
Provide a quiet low-stimulation space, reduce sensory input, allow time, and follow the support worker's guidance on his needs
Attempt verbal de-escalation using calm clear instructions and eye contact to re-orient him at this stage
Perform a CT brain to exclude acute neurological cause of his sudden non-verbal state at this stage

stem: A 30-year-old software developer with ASD Level 1 is referred by his GP for mental health review. He is highly skilled technically but has received performance warnings for not attending team meetings, avoiding client phone calls, and wearing noise-cancelling headphones at his desk which his manager finds rude. He describes the open-plan office as overwhelming. He is not depressed or anxious beyond workplace distress. He asks what medical letter he should request for his employer.

data_table.History: ASD Level 1. Software developer. Performance warnings for social avoidance and headphone use. No depression/anxiety beyond workplace.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.text: Suggest he find a different career better suited to his social communication profile and review clinical response at follow-up at this stage
Recommend he commence an SSRI for social anxiety to improve his workplace social functioning with regular monitoring of clinical parameters
Provide a letter recommending reasonable workplace adjustments under the Disability Discrimination Act including modified meeting participation and sensory accommodations
Refer for social skills training to improve his workplace interpersonal performance with close clinical monitoring throughout at this stage
Advise him that ASD does not qualify as a disability under employment law as he is high-functioning with appropriate specialist oversight

stem: A 31-year-old woman with schizophrenia well controlled on quetiapine 600 mg daily presents at 8 weeks gestation in a planned pregnancy. Her previous psychotic relapse (when she ceased medication independently) required 3 months inpatient admission. She and her partner have discussed the risks and want to continue medication. She asks which antipsychotic has the most pregnancy safety data.

data_table.History: Schizophrenia, one relapse requiring 3-month admission on medication cessation. Planned pregnancy.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate medication advice?

options.text: Reduce quetiapine to the minimum effective dose of 200 mg to minimise fetal exposure at this stage
Switch to haloperidol as typical antipsychotics have the longest overall pregnancy safety record
Continue quetiapine as it has the most pregnancy exposure data among atypical antipsychotics and she is stable on it
Cease quetiapine and manage with intensive psychological support throughout pregnancy at this stage
Switch to aripiprazole as it has the lowest metabolic side effects benefiting both mother and fetus

stem: A 26-year-old primigravida at 32 weeks gestation scores 14 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) administered by her midwife at routine antenatal visit. She endorsed item 10 (self-harm thoughts) as 'sometimes'. She appears tearful but denies active suicidal intent or plan. She has no psychiatric history and no substance use.

data_table.Screening: EPDS total 14/30. Item 10 (self-harm thoughts): 'Yes, quite often' (score 2/3).
data_table.History: Primigravida, 32 weeks. No psychiatric history. Supportive partner.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate psychiatric emergency assessment given endorsement of self-harm thoughts in pregnancy at this stage
Repeat the EPDS in two weeks as a single elevated score may represent normal pregnancy adjustment at this stage
Discuss item 10 further to assess risk, provide immediate psychosocial support, and arrange GP or perinatal mental health review within one week
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily as EPDS above 13 indicates antenatal depression requiring pharmacotherapy at this stage
Document the score and discuss at the next antenatal visit in 4 weeks as the midwife cannot initiate referral

stem: A 14-year-old presents to your general practice clinic accompanied by their mother. The adolescent reports a persistent and distressing sense that their experienced gender differs from their sex assigned at birth, present since age 10. They have been socially transitioning at school for the past 18 months with support from a school counsellor. The adolescent describes worsening distress related to the onset of puberty, with increasing body dissatisfaction, social withdrawal from peers, and declining academic performance over the past 6 months. There is no history of self-harm, substance use, or psychotic symptoms. The mother is supportive and wishes to understand the next steps in care.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Refer to a specialist multidisciplinary gender clinic for comprehensive assessment and discussion of treatment options
Continue monitoring in general practice with supportive counselling and reassess gender identity in 12 months before considering referral
Commence the adolescent on a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor targeting the depressive symptoms before considering gender-specific care
Refer to a child and adolescent psychiatrist for a general mental health assessment without specific gender clinic referral at this stage
Advise the family that gender identity typically resolves after puberty and recommend psychological therapy focused on acceptance of birth sex

stem:
A 28-year-old transgender woman presents to your clinic with a 3-month history of low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep, and reduced concentration. She has been on feminising hormone therapy with oral oestradiol valerate 6 mg daily and cyproterone acetate 12.5 mg daily for the past 2 years, prescribed by her endocrinologist. She has no prior psychiatric history. Her PHQ-9 score is 18 (severe range).

She is a non-smoker, drinks alcohol socially, and takes no other regular medications. Liver function tests and renal function are within normal limits. You diagnose major depressive disorder and plan to commence an antidepressant.
lead_in: Which antidepressant is the most appropriate first-line choice for this patient?

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg daily, given its long half-life provides stable plasma levels and it has a strong evidence base for depression
Sertraline 50 mg daily, given its favourable interaction profile with oestradiol and cyproterone acetate and strong efficacy evidence
Fluvoxamine 50 mg daily, as it is particularly effective for depressive disorders with prominent anxiety and sleep disturbance
Paroxetine 20 mg daily, as it has established efficacy and an anxiolytic profile that may help with the sleep disturbance component
Duloxetine 60 mg daily, as it provides dual serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibition which is preferable for more severe depression

subtopic_detail: Differential diagnosis in transgender patients post-transition
stem:
A 22-year-old transgender man presents to your outpatient clinic 4 months after bilateral mastectomy (top surgery). He reports persistent low mood, self-harm by cutting to his forearms (occurring 2-3 times per week for the past 6 weeks), and progressive social withdrawal. He describes feeling increasingly isolated after moving to a new city for work 3 months ago. He has experienced repeated workplace microaggressions related to his gender identity, including deliberate misgendering by a supervisor.

He reports intrusive thoughts about the workplace incidents but no flashbacks, nightmares, or hyperarousal symptoms. He denies dissociation. He had one prior episode of major depression at age 17, which was treated with sertraline and resolved within 8 months. He has been off antidepressants for 3 years. He reports satisfaction with his surgical outcome. He is on testosterone therapy and has no other medical conditions.
lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Adjustment disorder with depressed mood, precipitated by the relocation and workplace stressors within the past three months
Post-traumatic stress disorder related to chronic workplace discrimination, with re-experiencing and avoidance symptom clusters present
Recurrent major depressive disorder in the context of minority stress, exacerbated by social isolation and workplace gender-based discrimination
Gender dysphoria with residual distress following surgical transition, manifesting as depressive symptoms and regret-related self-harm
Testosterone-induced mood disturbance secondary to exogenous androgen therapy, requiring endocrinology review and dose adjustment first

subtopic: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander SEWB
stem:
A 32-year-old Aboriginal man is brought to a rural emergency department by police after being found wandering on a highway at night, speaking to unseen others and appearing distressed. He is from a remote community 200 km away and has been visiting family in the area. On assessment, he is agitated, describes hearing the voice of a recently deceased elder giving him instructions, and believes that a curse has been placed on him by a community member.

He has not slept for 3 days. There is no collateral history available, no known psychiatric history, and no evidence of substance use on urine drug screen. His vital signs are stable. The nursing staff have commenced de-escalation and he is now calmer but remains distressed. An Aboriginal Health Worker is available in the hospital.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in the assessment of this patient?

options.text: Commence oral olanzapine 10 mg for acute psychosis and arrange involuntary admission under the Mental Health Act given his risk behaviours
Perform a standard MSE and arrange a CT brain to exclude organic causes before proceeding with any further cultural assessment steps
Contact the local Aboriginal community-controlled health service and wait for their representative to attend before conducting any clinical assessment
Involve the Aboriginal Health Worker to assist with assessment, help determine the cultural context of his experiences, and facilitate contact with his family
Administer intramuscular droperidol 10 mg for acute behavioural disturbance and reassess once sedation allows a more thorough mental state examination

subtopic: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander SEWB
subtopic_detail: Perinatal mental health in Aboriginal women
stem:
A 24-year-old Aboriginal woman is seen at 6 weeks postpartum by her GP in a regional town. She was referred by the child health nurse who administered the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS), on which the patient scored 14. The patient describes feeling tired, overwhelmed, and tearful, with difficulty bonding with her baby. She reports that her mother-in-law has been critical of her parenting, and she feels disconnected from her own family, who live in a remote community 500 km away.

She is the primary carer for her two older children (aged 3 and 5). She has no prior psychiatric history and is not taking any medications. She is breastfeeding. An Aboriginal Maternal and Infant Health Service (AMIHS) operates in the region. She has a positive relationship with her AMIHS midwife, whom she has seen throughout pregnancy.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management approach?

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily as it is safe in breastfeeding, and arrange a follow-up appointment with the GP in two weeks to review response
Refer directly to a perinatal psychiatrist for specialist assessment given the EPDS score of 14 indicates moderate-severe postnatal depression
Readminister the EPDS in a culturally adapted format using validated Aboriginal-specific screening questions to confirm the screening result
Refer to the local perinatal mental health service for standard psychological therapy with cognitive behavioural therapy as the first-line intervention
Engage the AMIHS midwife in a collaborative care plan addressing social and cultural supports alongside clinical monitoring, and arrange follow-up

stem:
A 38-year-old man with a 15-year history of paranoid schizophrenia is reviewed by the community mental health team. He has had 6 involuntary admissions over the past 4 years, each precipitated by cessation of his depot paliperidone palmitate injection. Between admissions, he consistently stops attending for his depot within 2-3 months of discharge. During periods of non-adherence, he develops persecutory delusions, becomes verbally threatening to neighbours, and on one occasion was charged with assault.

When adherent to medication, he functions well in supported accommodation and denies ongoing psychotic symptoms. He has been assessed as having capacity to make treatment decisions when well, but consistently refuses ongoing depot medication once his symptoms resolve, stating he does not believe he has a mental illness. He is currently an inpatient following his most recent relapse and is responding well to reinitiated depot paliperidone.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition plan upon discharge?

options.text: Place on a Community Treatment Order mandating attendance for depot paliperidone injections and community mental health follow-up
Discharge on voluntary treatment with intensive community follow-up and assertive outreach to maximise medication adherence
Switch to oral risperidone to promote autonomy, with a clearly documented relapse prevention plan and early warning sign monitoring
Arrange long-term involuntary inpatient admission in a rehabilitation unit until the patient demonstrates sustained insight and voluntary adherence
Discharge to voluntary care with clozapine initiation to improve treatment response and reduce the likelihood of future non-adherence

stem:
You are a psychiatry registrar asked to assess a 29-year-old man in custody who has been charged with aggravated assault. He has a mild intellectual disability (IQ estimated at 62 on prior testing) and a diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder, currently partially treated with oral olanzapine 20 mg daily. His solicitor has requested a fitness to stand trial assessment, expressing concern that the defendant may not understand the court proceedings.

On interview, the man can state the name of the charge against him but cannot explain the possible outcomes of a guilty or not guilty plea. He believes his solicitor works for the police and is trying to trick him into confessing. He is unable to describe the roles of the judge, jury, or prosecution. He can follow simple two-step instructions.
lead_in: Which of the following is the most important element to assess when determining this man's fitness to stand trial?

options.text: Whether the defendant can give a reliable account of the events surrounding the alleged offence that is consistent with witness statements
Whether the defendant's intellectual disability is the primary cause of his impaired understanding rather than his psychotic illness alone
Whether the defendant is currently experiencing command auditory hallucinations that might influence his behaviour during the court proceedings
Whether the defendant has sufficient understanding of the nature of the charges, the court process, and the ability to communicate with and instruct his legal counsel
Whether the defendant's symptoms would be controlled sufficiently with optimised antipsychotic medication to render him fit before the scheduled trial date

subtopic_detail: Criteria for involuntary detention under the NSW Act
stem: A 42-year-old woman is brought to a NSW emergency department by her partner. She has not slept for 5 days, has spent $45,000 online and plans to fly overseas to pitch a business idea. She has bipolar I disorder with three prior manic episodes and stopped lithium 3 weeks ago. She is euphoric, grandiose and pressured, denies any problem and insists on leaving.

data_table.Collateral: No sleep for 5 days, $45,000 spent in one week, children aged 8 and 11 distressed

lead_in: Which combination of criteria must be met to detain her under the Act?

options.text: Mental illness, risk of harm, and her partner's written consent to treatment
Mentally ill person, risk of serious harm, no less restrictive care available
Formal capacity testing, a DSM-5 diagnosis, and two psychiatrists' recommendations
Treatment resistance, current refusal, and a previously attempted community order
Diagnosed illness, imminent danger to others, and documented voluntary options offered

stem:
A 34-year-old woman presents to your outpatient clinic after her second episode of bipolar depression in 2 years. She was diagnosed with bipolar II disorder 3 years ago. Her hypomanic episodes have been brief (lasting 4-5 days) and have not caused significant functional impairment or required hospitalisation. Her depressive episodes, however, have been prolonged (each lasting 3-4 months) and severely disabling, with one requiring a 2-week period off work.

She is currently euthymic following treatment of her most recent depressive episode with quetiapine, which she wishes to discontinue due to weight gain of 8 kg. She has no other medical conditions. She is using reliable contraception and does not plan pregnancy in the near future. She asks about long-term medication to prevent further depressive episodes.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line mood stabiliser for long-term prophylaxis in this patient?

options.text: Lithium carbonate, titrated to a serum level of 0.6-0.8 mmol/L, given its strong evidence base across all phases of bipolar disorder
Sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily, given its broad-spectrum mood stabilising properties and efficacy in both manic and depressive episodes
Lamotrigine, titrated slowly to 200 mg daily over 6-8 weeks, given its established efficacy for preventing depressive relapse in bipolar II disorder
Quetiapine at a reduced dose of 150 mg at night, to maintain prophylaxis while minimising the metabolic side effects she has experienced
Carbamazepine 200 mg twice daily, as it provides mood stabilisation with a lower risk of weight gain compared to quetiapine or valproate

stem:
A 41-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has been on lithium monotherapy for 2 years, maintained at a serum level of 0.75 mmol/L. Despite adherence (confirmed by consistent therapeutic levels), he has experienced 5 mood episodes in the past 12 months: 3 depressive episodes and 2 manic episodes, each lasting 2-4 weeks. He has no substance use disorder, and thyroid function is normal (TSH 2.1 mIU/L).

His most recent episode was a manic episode that resolved 3 weeks ago. He also takes atorvastatin for hyperlipidaemia. Renal function is normal. He is currently euthymic and asks what changes can be made to reduce the frequency of his episodes.

data_table.Current medications: Lithium carbonate 900 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in pharmacological management?

options.text: Add sodium valproate titrated to a serum level of 350-700 micromol/L while continuing lithium at the current dose and monitoring for interactions
Discontinue lithium and switch to carbamazepine 400 mg twice daily, as carbamazepine is the preferred agent for rapid cycling presentations
Add lamotrigine titrated to 200 mg daily while continuing lithium, as lamotrigine addresses the predominant depressive pole of his cycling
Increase lithium to achieve a serum level of 1.0-1.2 mmol/L before considering adjunctive therapy, as higher levels may improve rapid cycling control
Add quetiapine 300 mg daily while continuing lithium, as atypical antipsychotics are preferred adjuncts for rapid cycling due to their rapid onset

stem:
A 36-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder presents to the emergency department with a 10-day history of elevated mood, reduced sleep (3 hours per night with no daytime fatigue), grandiosity, and increased goal-directed activity. However, she simultaneously reports intense feelings of hopelessness, guilt about neglecting her children, and fleeting suicidal ideation without plan or intent. She is tearful during parts of the interview yet pressured and grandiose in others.

She is not currently on any psychiatric medication, having self-discontinued lithium and quetiapine 2 months ago. She has no substance use. Her BMI is 23 kg/m2. She has no other medical conditions and takes no regular medications.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment for the acute management of this presentation?

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg daily combined with lithium carbonate, to simultaneously address both the depressive and manic components of this episode
Lithium carbonate monotherapy titrated to 0.8-1.0 mmol/L, as it remains the gold standard for acute mania with additional antisuicidal properties
Carbamazepine 400 mg daily, titrated to therapeutic levels, given its efficacy in mixed states and its favourable metabolic profile for this patient
Olanzapine 10-15 mg daily or sodium valproate titrated to therapeutic levels, as both have established efficacy for manic episodes with mixed features
Lamotrigine titrated to 200 mg over 6 weeks, given its dual efficacy for both depressive and manic symptoms and the need for a mood stabiliser with a benign side effect profile

stem:
A 48-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been stable on clozapine 400 mg daily for 3 years, with a trough level of 420 mcg/L (therapeutic range 350-600 mcg/L). He presents to the GP with dysuria and urinary frequency. Urine culture confirms Escherichia coli urinary tract infection. The GP prescribes ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days. Three days later, the patient presents to the emergency department drowsy, drooling excessively, and tachycardic (heart rate 110 bpm).

His blood pressure is 100/65 mmHg. He is afebrile. His family reports he has been increasingly sedated over the past 2 days and had a witnessed seizure this morning.
lead_in: What is the most likely cause of this patient's presentation?

options.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome precipitated by an interaction between ciprofloxacin and clozapine that has altered dopamine receptor sensitivity
Sepsis secondary to clozapine-induced agranulocytosis, with the urinary tract infection being the source, leading to deterioration despite antibiotic therapy
Clozapine-associated myocarditis presenting with tachycardia and hypotension, coincidentally occurring during the course of antibiotic treatment for the infection
Ciprofloxacin-induced lowering of seizure threshold in combination with the inherent epileptogenic properties of clozapine at standard therapeutic doses
Clozapine toxicity caused by ciprofloxacin inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism, resulting in significantly elevated clozapine serum levels and dose-dependent adverse effects

stem:
A 27-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on carbamazepine 600 mg daily for the past 18 months. She presents to your clinic requesting contraception. She is in a new relationship and has been using condoms inconsistently. She has no desire for pregnancy in the next 3-5 years. Her mood has been stable with no episodes since starting carbamazepine.

She has previously trialled lithium (discontinued due to tremor and weight gain) and valproate (discontinued due to hair loss and concern about teratogenicity). She is otherwise well, takes no other medications, and has a BMI of 24 kg/m2. She asks about starting the combined oral contraceptive pill.

data_table.Prior medications trialled: Lithium (tremor, weight gain), valproate (hair loss, teratogenicity concern)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding contraception for this patient?

options.text: Prescribe the combined oral contraceptive pill at standard dose, as modern formulations have sufficient oestrogen content to maintain efficacy with carbamazepine
Prescribe a higher-dose combined oral contraceptive pill containing at least 50 mcg ethinylestradiol to overcome the enzyme induction effect of carbamazepine
Recommend a copper intrauterine device or levonorgestrel intrauterine system, as these long-acting methods are unaffected by hepatic enzyme induction
Switch carbamazepine to lamotrigine, which does not induce hepatic enzymes, so that a combined oral contraceptive pill can be prescribed safely
Recommend the etonogestrel subdermal implant, as it provides long-acting contraception and its progestogen levels are sufficient to overcome enzyme induction effects

stem:
A 45-year-old woman presents to your clinic with a 4-month history of difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep. She was diagnosed with major depressive disorder 12 months ago and has been stable on sertraline 100 mg daily for the past 8 months, with a PHQ-9 score of 4 (minimal symptoms). Despite her mood improvement, she continues to take more than 45 minutes to fall asleep most nights and wakes 2-3 times per night, resulting in daytime fatigue and difficulty concentrating at work.

She has been using her phone in bed, drinking 2-3 cups of coffee daily (last at 3 pm), and napping for 30-60 minutes in the afternoon on weekends. She does not snore and has no symptoms of restless legs. She does not use alcohol. She has tried over-the-counter melatonin 2 mg for 2 weeks without benefit.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment for this patient's insomnia?

options.text: Increase sertraline to 150 mg daily, as the residual insomnia likely represents incomplete treatment of her underlying depressive disorder
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, which addresses the perpetuating behavioural and cognitive factors maintaining her sleep disturbance
Prescribe zopiclone 7.5 mg at night for 2 weeks to re-establish a sleep pattern, with a plan to taper once regular sleep is restored
Switch sertraline to mirtazapine 15 mg at night, as its sedating properties will treat both the residual depressive symptoms and the insomnia
Prescribe prolonged-release melatonin 2 mg at night for 3 months, as the previous trial was too brief to assess efficacy of melatonin treatment

subtopic_detail: Reduced sleep need versus insomnia in bipolar disorder
stem:
A 33-year-old man with bipolar I disorder, stable on lithium carbonate 1000 mg daily (serum level 0.72 mmol/L), is reviewed in your outpatient clinic. His partner has accompanied him and reports that over the past 10 days he has been sleeping only 3-4 hours per night. When asked about this, the patient states he feels well-rested and full of energy despite the reduced sleep.

He has started a new creative project, working on it from 4 am each morning, and describes his ideas as brilliant and groundbreaking. He is speaking faster than usual and is mildly irritable when his partner expresses concern. He denies low mood, anxiety, or substance use. He reports no change in appetite or physical symptoms. His lithium level was checked 5 days ago and was 0.72 mmol/L. He denies caffeine increase and has not recently changed medications.
lead_in: What is the most likely explanation for this patient's change in sleep pattern?

options.text: Primary insomnia disorder developing independently of his bipolar disorder, given his lithium level is within the therapeutic range and he reports feeling well
Lithium-induced sleep disruption due to polyuria and nocturia, which is a common adverse effect at therapeutic serum levels in long-term lithium treatment
Stimulant substance use that the patient is concealing, as the presentation of reduced sleep with increased energy and productivity is most consistent with amphetamine use
Emerging hypomanic or manic relapse, as the reduced need for sleep with preserved energy is a core feature of bipolar mood elevation and an early warning sign
Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder (advanced sleep phase type), as the consistent 4 am wakening suggests an abnormally advanced circadian clock cycle

stem:
A 31-year-old woman presents to your clinic 7 months after a motor vehicle accident in which she was a restrained front-seat passenger. She sustained a fractured clavicle, which has healed. She describes intrusive memories of the accident occurring daily, vivid nightmares 3-4 times per week, avoidance of driving and travelling on highways, hypervigilance when a passenger in cars, and an exaggerated startle response to sudden noises.

She has become socially withdrawn, stopped attending her gym, and has difficulty concentrating at work. She meets DSM-5 criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder. She has no prior psychiatric history, takes no medications, and does not use alcohol or other substances. She is motivated to engage in treatment and asks about her options.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment for this patient?

options.text: Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy, typically delivered over 8-12 sessions with a structured exposure and cognitive restructuring component
Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing therapy, delivered over 8-12 sessions as the preferred modality for motor vehicle accident trauma
Sertraline 50 mg daily titrated to 100-200 mg as tolerated, as pharmacotherapy should precede psychological therapy to reduce symptom severity first
Supportive psychotherapy focused on building coping skills and resilience, as trauma-focused approaches should be reserved for treatment-resistant cases
Combined sertraline 50 mg daily and trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy from treatment commencement for optimal synergistic benefit

stem:
A 38-year-old refugee woman from East Africa is referred to your outpatient clinic by her GP. She experienced childhood sexual abuse from age 6 to 12, witnessed community violence, and spent 3 years in a refugee camp before resettlement in Australia 2 years ago. She reports a 5-year relationship with a partner who is physically and verbally abusive; she remains in the relationship and states she cannot leave due to financial dependence and fear.

She describes pervasive feelings of emptiness, shame, difficulty trusting others, chronic emotional dysregulation with anger outbursts, and interpersonal difficulties. She has nightmares 4-5 times per week, avoids any reminders of her past, and dissociates during stressful interactions (described as going blank for minutes at a time). She was previously trialled on 16 sessions of standard trauma-focused CBT by a psychologist, which was discontinued after 8 sessions due to severe dissociation during imaginal exposure and worsening self-harm. She is currently on sertraline 150 mg daily with partial benefit for mood and anxiety. Her PHQ-9 is 14 and her PCL-5 is 62.

data_table.Prior therapy trial: TF-CBT - 8 of 16 sessions, discontinued (dissociation, worsening self-harm)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate therapeutic approach at this stage?

options.text: Resume trauma-focused CBT with a different therapist, using a slower titration of exposure and with grounding techniques incorporated into each session
Commence EMDR therapy as it is better tolerated than TF-CBT in patients with dissociative symptoms, as it does not require sustained imaginal exposure
Increase sertraline to 200 mg daily and add prazosin 1-2 mg at night for nightmare reduction, deferring all psychological therapy until pharmacological optimisation
Commence cognitive processing therapy, as it focuses on cognitive restructuring of trauma-related beliefs without requiring imaginal exposure to specific traumatic memories
Implement a phase-based approach beginning with safety planning, emotional regulation skills, and dissociation management, before introducing any trauma-focused processing

subtopic_detail: SSRI choice in chronic liver disease
stem:
A 56-year-old man is referred to your outpatient clinic by his hepatologist for management of major depressive disorder. He has a history of alcohol-related liver cirrhosis, currently classified as Child-Pugh B (score 8). He achieved abstinence from alcohol 9 months ago with the support of an addiction medicine specialist. He describes 3 months of persistent low mood, anhedonia, early morning wakening, poor appetite with 5 kg unintentional weight loss, fatigue, and feelings of worthlessness.

His PHQ-9 is 17. He has no suicidal ideation. His current medications include spironolactone 100 mg daily and lactulose. He has no known drug allergies. He has not previously been prescribed antidepressants.
lead_in: Which antidepressant is the most appropriate first-line choice for this patient?

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg daily, given its long half-life provides stable plasma levels and it has a well-established evidence base for major depression
Duloxetine 60 mg daily, given its dual mechanism provides superior efficacy for moderate-severe depression and it has a favourable interaction profile
Sertraline at a reduced starting dose of 25 mg daily, given its relatively lower hepatic extraction ratio and established safety profile in liver disease
Paroxetine 20 mg daily, as it is the most potent SSRI and therefore most likely to achieve treatment response at the lowest possible effective dose
Mirtazapine 15 mg at night, as its sedating and appetite-stimulating properties are particularly beneficial given his insomnia and weight loss presentation
